label: Psychology
title: Flow – The Psychology of Losing Yourself in What You Do
description: Some hours vanish in what feels like minutes. You are absorbed, focused, and strangely calm. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent decades studying these moments and called them flow. In this calm video essay we look at how he discovered flow, the beeper studies that tracked thousands of ordinary moments, why the balance between challenge and skill matters so much, what constant distraction does to our attention, and why Aristotle had a surprisingly similar idea about happiness more than two thousand years earlier.

sections.text:
You sit down to do something. Maybe you are drawing, or writing, or fixing a bicycle, or playing a piece of music. And then, at some point, you look up. The light outside has changed. Two hours have passed, and they felt like twenty minutes.

You were not thinking about yourself. You were not checking your phone. You were simply there, inside what you were doing.

Most of us have known moments like this. And one psychologist spent most of his life asking a simple question about them. What exactly is happening, and why do these moments feel so good?

sections.heading: The Painters Who Forgot to Eat
sections.text:
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi was born in 1934, in a city on the Adriatic coast that is now Rijeka in Croatia. As a child he lived through the Second World War, and he later said that he saw many adults lose everything they had relied on. Some of them fell apart. A few somehow stayed calm and purposeful. He wanted to understand the difference.

Years later, as a young researcher in Chicago, he studied artists at work. He noticed something puzzling. The painters were completely absorbed while working. They would forget to eat, forget the time, ignore discomfort. But once a painting was finished, many of them lost interest in it almost immediately and started the next one.

So the reward was not the finished picture. It seemed to be the painting itself.

He went on to interview climbers, dancers, chess players, surgeons and many others. And again and again, people described the best moments of their activity with the same image. It felt, they said, like being carried by a current. Like flow.

Csikszentmihalyi kept working on these questions until his death in 2021.

sections.heading: Catching Ordinary Moments
sections.text:
Asking people to remember their best experiences is useful, but memory is unreliable. So Csikszentmihalyi and his colleagues, among them Reed Larson, developed a different method.

They gave participants pagers. At random moments during the day, the pager would beep. Each time, the person stopped and wrote down where they were, what they were doing, and how they felt. How focused, how happy, how motivated.

This became known as the experience sampling method. Over the years, studies of this kind gathered a very large number of snapshots of ordinary life, from teenagers, workers and older adults.

And they produced a surprising pattern. In one well-known study, Csikszentmihalyi and Judith LeFevre found that people reported flow-like experiences more often at work than in their free time. Yet at work, they also said they wished they were somewhere else. In their leisure hours, much of which was spent passively, they often felt relaxed but also flat and unfocused.

We tend to assume that rest makes us happiest. The beeper studies suggested that something more active may matter just as much.

sections.heading: Between Anxiety and Boredom
sections.text:
So what creates flow? In his book Flow, published in 1990, Csikszentmihalyi described several conditions that tend to appear together.

The most important is a balance between challenge and skill. If a task is far too hard for us, we feel anxious. If it is far too easy, we feel bored. Flow tends to appear in the narrow channel between the two, when a task asks a little more of us than we are used to, but not too much.

And this channel moves. As our skills grow, the old challenge becomes easy, and boredom creeps in. To find flow again, we have to raise the challenge. In this way, Csikszentmihalyi thought, flow quietly pulls us toward growth. We keep returning to the edge of what we can do.

It also helps to have clear goals, so you know what you are trying to do next. And immediate feedback, so you can tell whether it is working. A climber feels every hold. A musician hears every note.

When these conditions come together, people describe similar experiences. Deep concentration. A loss of self-consciousness, as if the inner critic has gone quiet. A changed sense of time. And a feeling that the activity is worth doing for its own sake.

Csikszentmihalyi called such activities autotelic, from the Greek for having its goal in itself.

sections.heading: The Enemy of Flow
sections.text:
Flow needs one thing above all. Uninterrupted attention. And that may be the thing that is hardest to find today.

Every notification, every quick glance at a message, pulls us out of the current. And getting back in is not instant. The management researcher Sophie Leroy described what she called attention residue. When we switch from one task to another, part of our mind tends to stay with the task we left. In her experiments, people who switched with an unfinished task still on their mind did worse on the next one.

So a day of constant small interruptions may not just cost us the minutes we spend on our phones. It can keep us hovering at the surface, never deep enough for flow to begin.

This does not mean technology is bad, or that we should feel guilty. It simply means that deep focus rarely happens by accident. It usually needs a little protection.

sections.heading: Aristotle's Activity

quote.lead: More than two thousand years before the beeper studies, Aristotle asked what a good human life consists of. In his Nicomachean Ethics, he concludes:
quote.text: Human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue.
quote.author: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7, 1098a – transl. W. D. Ross (1908)

sections.text:
The key word is activity. For Aristotle, happiness was not a feeling we receive, or a possession we keep. It was something we do. A life of using our abilities well, fully, and with care.

He even had an image for pleasure. In a later book of the Ethics, he says that pleasure completes an activity, a little like the bloom of youth on a person in their prime. The pleasure is not the goal. It is what naturally appears when an activity is done well.

Csikszentmihalyi's research seems to point in a similar direction. The best moments of our lives are often not the most passive or the most comfortable ones. They are the moments when we are fully engaged in something that asks us to stretch.

sections.heading: Making Room for Flow
sections.text:
You cannot force flow. But you can make room for it.

Choose one activity that you care about, and give it a protected block of time. Even forty-five minutes can be enough. Put the phone in another room, not just face down on the table.

Adjust the challenge. If you feel bored, make the task a little harder. Set yourself a time, a new technique, a higher standard. If you feel overwhelmed, make it smaller. One page, one paragraph, one bar of music.

Make the next step clear. Before you begin, decide exactly what you are going to do first. Vague goals tend to invite distraction.

And notice the moment after. When you look up and the light has changed, pay attention to how you feel. That quiet satisfaction is worth remembering, because it tells you something about what a good day can look like.

Not a day with nothing to do. A day with something worth doing, and the space to disappear into it.

short.hook: Why do some hours vanish in minutes?
short.title: The psychology of losing track of time
short.text:
You look up, and two hours have passed. They felt like twenty minutes.

The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called this flow. To study it, he gave people pagers that beeped at random moments. Each time, they wrote down what they were doing and how they felt.

The pattern was surprising. People reported flow more often at work than in their free time.

Flow tends to appear between anxiety and boredom, when a task asks a little more of us than we are used to.

So choose one thing you care about. Put your phone in another room. And let yourself disappear into it.
